attributes.title: Level 5

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you create an image asset then resize the canvas to 16x32?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What do you notice about how the pixels are positioned in the outline of the sword image?

❓ Why might it be useful to draw a blank outline when creating pixel art?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Point out to the ninja that a pixel art outline should have clear lines. Have the ninja notice that the pixels in the sword image have clear, straight edges to make it pop on the project screen. Later, the ninja will edit the outline so that there are the same number of pixels on each step of the line, and the pixels are connected diagonally.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by drawing the outline of a sword image. 


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen. Create a new image asset called sword0. Change the canvas size to be 16x32.


Use the paint tool to draw an outline of a sword, like this:

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the fill tool to color in the sword blade and hilt?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might light purple and yellow be used as the base colors of the sword image?

❓ What other colors might be added to enhance the sword image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Because there are only 15 colors in MakeCode’s paint editor, colors need to be strategically used to mimic what it would look like in real life. For example, the blade of the sword would likely be metal, presenting as silver or gray in real life. Because there is no gray in MakeCode’s paint editor, alternative colors need to be used.
steps.instructions:
Add base colors to the sword image!


Duplicate the sword0 asset, then rename the new asset sword1. 


Use the fill tool to add a base color inside the sword outline. Use light purple (11) to color the blade of the sword. Use yellow (5) to color the hilt, or the handle of the sword. 


The sword image might look like this:

steps.hints: ❓Did you add highlights and shadows by drawing vertical lines inside the outline of the sword blade?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What are highlights and shadows used for in pixel art?

❓ Why does it matter where the light source is when adding highlights and shadows to an image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Highlights and shadows create more depth in a pixel art image. This makes the object seem as if it’s three dimensional, rather than just a flat image on screen.

💡 The light source is important because it determines where to place the highlights and shadows. In this example, the light source is coming from the left side, creating a highlight on the left part of the sword and a shadow on the right side.
steps.instructions:
Add shading to the blade of the sword image!


Duplicate the sword1 asset, then rename the new asset sword2.


Use the paint or the line tool to add highlights and shadows to the blade of the sword.


The light source in this image will be coming from the left side of the canvas, and will shine across the sword, creating a highlight on the left part of the sword and a shadow on the right side.


Draw a vertical line in white (1) to highlight the left side of the blade, and in dark purple (12) to add a shadow to the right side of the blade, both inside the outline of the sword.


The sword image might look like this:

steps.hints: ❓Did you use tan to highlight and orange to add shadows to the hilt of the sword image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓Why might tan be used as the highlight on the hilt, and orange be used as the shadow? 

❓Where should pixels be placed on the hilt to create highlights and shadows?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Highlights should be added in a color lighter than the base color. Shadows should be added in a color darker than the base color. Because the base color of the hilt is yellow, tan and orange can be used as the highlight and shadow.

💡 Remind the ninja that the light source in this image is coming from the left, so the highlight should be placed on the left side of the hilt and the shadow should be placed on the right side.
steps.instructions:
Add shading to the hilt of the sword image!


Duplicate the sword2 asset, then rename the new asset sword3.


Use the paint or the line tool to add highlights and shadows to the sword’s hilt. Use tan (13) to highlight the left side of the hilt, inside the outlines. Use orange (4) to add shadows to the right side of the hilt, both inside the outline of the sword.


Use other colors to decorate the middle of the hilt with a gemstone or other design.


The sword image might look like this:

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the erase tool to remove extra pixels in the outline, like the red pixels in this image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is a “jaggy” in pixel art? Why should they be removed?

❓ Where might dark purple be used to smooth the edges of the sword image?

❓ What other finishing touches might be added to the sword image?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 A “jaggy” is a break in a smooth line in an image. This often occurs when there are multiple pixels that are part of a line, rather than just one. Prompt the ninja to notice where pixels are connected linearly, rather than diagonally, and where pixels can be erased to create a smoother outline.
steps.instructions:
Edit the outline to smooth the edges of the sword image!


Duplicate the sword3 asset, then rename the new asset sword4.


Notice the lines of the sword asset and look for “jaggies”, or a break in a smooth line in the image. Use the erase tool to remove extra pixels around the edges of the sword to make them less “pointy”. 


Look for areas of the outline where softer colors, such as dark purple, can be used to make the image appear more smooth. For example, use dark purple on the left outline of the blade.


Add any other finishing touches to the sword image before code is added to display it on the project screen!


The finished sword image might look like this:

steps.hints: ❓Did you type assets, a dot operator, the asset type and the asset name inside 2 backticks `` for each element in the swordArray?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you place the sword image assets in the correct order in the swordArray?

❓ What background image might be used to display the sword images on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the number of each image asset matches the corresponding index in the array so that each image builds on the previous one.
steps.instructions:
Set the scene to display the sword images on screen!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add a // project initialization comment at the top. Below, declare a swordArray to store the 5 sword image assets.


Then, add a // project start comment and set a background color or image underneath. 


Click ▶ to see the chosen background image appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add an xOffset value (25) with a spacing value (25), multiplied by the counter variable i like this: (25 + (25 * i)), to set each sprite’s x-position?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What values might be used to offset the sprites from the left side of the screen and to space out each sprite?

❓ How do the sword images appear on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out their code to make sure the sprites are placed correctly on screen. Prompt them to consider which values should be added together and which should be multiplied to correctly position the images.

💡 Point out to the ninja that they made small updates to the sword image in each iteration. Have them compare the first and last images to see how the drawing progressed over time.
steps.instructions:
Display the sword image from each step of the drawing process on screen!


Under // project start, use a for loop to create 5 sprites. Use the loop’s counter variable to select a different image from the swordArray, each time the loop runs.


Set the x-position of the sprites by adding a value to offset the left side of the screen with the spacing between each sprite, multiplied by the counter variable. Set the y-position to a coordinate in the middle of the screen.


Click ▶ to see each sword image displayed on screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you update all 4 parameters in the runImageAnimation function so that the images in the swordArray continuously loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might the runImageAnimation function be useful for showing multiple iterations of an image?

❓ What might the frameInterval and loop parameters be set to so that the images continuously rotate at a reasonable rate?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The runImageAnimation function can be useful for showing how an image changes over time. In this context, because the sword image was slowly added onto, the image animation helps the user visualize how it transformed in each version.
steps.instructions:
Add image animation to show the progression across the sword images!


Under // project start, create a new sprite with its image set to the first element of the swordArray. Position the sprite to appear above the 5 sprites created in the for loop.


Animate the sprite’s image to rotate through each of the elements in the swordArray. Update the frameInterval and loop parameters so that the images continuously cycle through.


Click ▶ to see the progression of the sword image on screen!

subgroups.title: Creating Custom Pixel Art
subgroups.introduction: Create and refine an original pixel art image in the MakeCode image editor.

validationItems.text: Store 5 unique sword image assets in a swordArray list.
Place the 5 sword images on screen using a for loop.
Animate a sprite that cycles through the 5 images.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 5 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about creating original pixel art images. You’ll be able to take the strategies you learn in this level to create detailed assets in future projects! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 5:

badges.title: Pixel Artist
badges.description: Use a variety of pixel art techniques to create original pixel art assets to be used in a project.

badges.title: Work of Art
badges.description: Create and refine original pixel art images in the MakeCode paint editor.

badges.title: Neat n’ Tidy
badges.description: Create smooth outlines by removing jaggies in a pixel art image.

badges.title: Color Wheel
badges.description: Use analogous or complementary colors to modify the level of contrast in a pixel art image.

badges.title: Depth Perception
badges.description: Add highlights and shadows to make a pixel art image look realistic.

badges.title: I’m Dithering Away!
badges.description: Use dithering to ease the transition between colors in a pixel art image.

badges.title: Up to Scale
badges.description: Create and refine multiple sizes of a pixel art image.
